title: He calls her mother
hookLine: Bhishma calls his father's bride mother and brings her home himself: matru devo bhava
carry: matru devo bhava: honor a mother as god

cards: The fisherman has given his consent, before the old chiefs who came with the prince. The flowers have stopped falling.
And the young prince turns to the fisherman's daughter, the woman he has just won as a bride for his father, and speaks to her as her son. Mother, he says, get into my chariot, and let's go home.
With one word, the vow becomes something you can see.

teach.b: He doesn't send her with servants. He helps her into his own chariot and takes her himself, to Hastinapura, the Kuru capital. There he tells his father all of it: the condition, the throne, the vow.
The text says the kings who heard what he had done praised it, and said it too: he is truly Bhishma. Now notice that word, mother. An hour ago she was the price of a bargain.

She's a fisherman's daughter, close to his own age. With one word he gives her a mother's honor, and steps into a family that will grow around him and never through him. The Taittiriya Upanishad has a line in four parts.
Matru devo bhava: let your mother be like God to you. Then father, teacher and guest. This week we've met a teacher, Vasishtha, and a father, Shantanu; today a mother, chosen.
In Hinduism, mother is a word of honor before it's anything else.
Hindus call the Goddess Ma: Durga Ma, Ganga Ma. Older women are Mataji or Auntie.

A new bride often calls her husband's mother Ma or Mummy-ji. The word isn't only about who gave birth to you; it's how you decide to treat someone. Eight days ago in our reading, he was a baby carried off by a river.
Today he brings a new mother home to his father, with a whole life of keeping that vow still ahead of him.

how: Some Hindus address goddesses, elders and respected women as Mata or Ma, mother, a word of honor as well as of kinship.

o: Devavrata's promise, lived at once as a son to his father's bride
the kings' oath to crown the fisherman's grandson one day
a promise to drive his father's bride home in a royal parade

games.q: the ride home — tap the pairs.
p: he took her home in his own
let your mother be like God

s: in Hinduism, 'mother' is only for the woman who gave birth to you
Hindus call the Goddess, elders and a husband's mother Ma: it's a word of honor.
Bhishma called his father's bride mother
he said to her: mother, get into my chariot.
Bhishma kept his vows secret from his father
he told Shantanu all of it when they arrived.

games.q: you're Bhishma. you've just won the fisherman's daughter as your father's bride. how do you speak to her?
o: you leave the talking to the elders.
games.why: he calls her mother and takes her home himself. with one word, the vow becomes a family.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's family to you by choice rather than by birth: a stepparent, an in-law, a godparent, an elder you call auntie.
Breathe in and think of the word that says what they are to you; breathe out and let that word rest in the chest. If you pray, ask a blessing for them.
If no one comes to mind, hold the people you'd like to be that kind of family to.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma's vow. Kept from the first moment, in a single word to the woman he brought home: mother.

orig.note: Sanskrit mātā, mother: what Bhishma calls the bride he brings home.

carryVoice: Your line: matru devo bhava, honor a mother as God. Tomorrow, a father's gift. That's day seven hundred fourteen.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Bhishma brings the fisherman's daughter to Hastinapura; the kings praise him)
